title: Book 6 — Erato, Chapter 103
paragraphs: When the Athenians learned of this, they too marched out to Marathon to defend their territory, led by ten generals. The tenth of these was Miltiades, whose father Cimon son of Stesagoras had been forced to go into exile from Athens on account of Pisistratus son of Hippocrates. While in exile, Cimon happened to win a victory at the Olympic games with the four-horse chariot, matching in this achievement his half-brother Miltiades, who had the same mother. Then at the next Olympics he won again with the same mares but allowed Pisistratus to be proclaimed the victor; by handing over the victory he was permitted to return home under an agreement for peace. After he had won yet again at a later Olympic festival with the same mares, it was his fate to be killed by the sons of Pisistratus — Pisistratus himself being no longer alive. They sent men to ambush him by night near the City Hall and had him killed there. Cimon's grave is in the outer part of the city, across the road called the Hollow Way, and directly opposite him are buried those mares that had won him three Olympic victories. The mares of Euagoras the Laconian achieved the same feat, but no others did. Now at that time the elder of Cimon's sons, Stesagoras, was being raised in the house of his uncle Miltiades in the Chersonese, while the younger was being brought up at Athens with Cimon himself, bearing the name Miltiades after Miltiades the founder of the colony in the Chersonese.
